method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry and caption. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch10 p756-761: auto-generated source checklist from existing 78 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 3x zoom; any printed unit errors or ambiguous glyphs are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan.

elements.source: The six presentations of glomerular disease listed are asymptomatic, macrohematuria, nephrotic syndrome and: [Presentations: asymptomatic, macrohematuria, nephrotic syndrome, nephritic syndrome (acute GN), RPGN, CKD (chronic GN). (Book p756)]

Match each pattern with its book label — 1) Nephritic syndrome 2) CKD of glomerular disease 3) CKD of vascular disease … A) Ischemic nephropathy B) CKD CGN (chronic glomerulonephritis) C) Acute glomerulonephritis [Nephritic syndrome = acute GN; CKD of glomerular disease = CKD CGN; CKD of vascular disease = ischemic nephropathy. (Book p756)]
The m/c presentation that heads the biopsy-indication flowchart is: [Asymptomatic urine abnormalities (m/c presentation) lead to biopsy. (Book p756)]

Asymptomatic urine abnormalities go to biopsy with proteinuria above 500 mg/24 hrs plus microhematuria of at least: [Proteinuria (>500 mg/24 hrs) + microhematuria (≥3 RBC/HPF); proteinuria alone >1 g/24 hrs → biopsy. (Book p756)]

Fill up: In the macrohematuria 40/5/1 rule, the "1" stands for one ______ plus significant proteinuria. [40/5/1 rule: ≥40 dysmorphic, ≥5 acanthocytes, 1 RBC cast + significant proteinuria → biopsy. (Book p756)]
Match each number of the macrohematuria rule with its finding — 1) ≥40 2) ≥5 3) 1 … A) RBC cast B) Dysmorphic RBCs C) Acanthocytes [≥40: dysmorphic; ≥5: acanthocytes; 1: RBC cast. (Book p756)]

Which of these is NOT one of the six numbered presentations of glomerular disease on this page? [The list is 1. Asymptomatic, 2. macrohematuria, 3. nephrotic syndrome, 4. nephritic syndrome (acute glomerulonephritis), 5. RPGN, 6. chronic kidney di]

Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria are noted on this page as having previously formed part of the diagnostic criteria for nephrotic syndrome. [Beneath the three printed criteria the note reads: 'Hyperlipidemia, lipiduria were previously part of diagnostic criteria'. (Book p756)]

Fill up: The third criterion of nephrotic syndrome is oedema, which the page describes as ______ oedema. [Criterion 3 is written as 'Edema : Extravascular', with 1 Nephrotic range proteinuria and 2 Hypoalbuminemia <3 g/dl. (Book p756)]

A 6-year-old has nephrotic-range proteinuria, serum albumin 3.4 g/dL and periorbital puffiness. Applying the criteria box, this child: [The bracket beside the criteria prints 'Adults: 1 + 2 + 3' and 'Children: 1 + 2 or 3', so criterion 1 with edema alone satisfies the paediatric defini]

In the biopsy-indication flowchart, proteinuria ALONE prompts biopsy once it exceeds: [The asymptomatic arm lists two routes: proteinuria >500 mg/24 hrs plus microhematuria ≥3 RBC/HPF, or proteinuria alone >1 g/24 hrs. (Book p756)]
The nephrotic syndrome criteria are nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and extravascular edema; the combination required in adults is: [Adults: 1 + 2 + 3; children: 1 + 2 or 3. (Book p756)]
The hypoalbuminemia cut-off in the nephrotic criteria is serum albumin below: [Hypoalbuminemia: < 3 g/dl. (Book p756)]
Which statement about the diagnostic criteria is TRUE? [Note: hyperlipidemia, lipiduria were previously part of diagnostic criteria; edema is extravascular. (Book p756)]
Nephrotic-range proteinuria by total protein is >3500 mg/24 hrs in adults and, in children: [Total protein: adults >3500 mg/24 hrs; children >50 mg/kg/day. (Book p756)]

elements.source: The urine protein creatinine ratio (PCR) nephrotic-range cut-offs are: [Urine PCR: adult ≥3000 mg/g; children ≥2000 mg/g. (Book p757)]
Which statement about the urine PCR is TRUE as written? [Not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome. (Book p757)]

Nephrotic-range proteinuria is "also seen in" diabetes (m/c), 2° FSGS and amyloidosis; the treatment bracketed for this group is: [Also seen in: diabetes (m/c), 2° FSGS, amyloidosis → Rx: ACE inhibitors, ARB. (Book p757)]
In childhood nephrotic syndrome the edema compartment relationship written is: [Proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + edema; extravascular > intravascular. (Book p757)]

The bracket drawn after the 'Also seen in' causes carries which printed advice? [Nephrotic-range proteinuria is also seen in diabetes (m/c), secondary FSGS and amyloidosis, and the bracket beside that group reads 'Rx: ACE inhibitor]

A raised urine protein–creatinine ratio is explicitly described on this page as not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome. [The PCR block gives adult ≥3000 mg/g and children ≥2000 mg/g, then the line 'Not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome'. (Book p757)]

A diabetic with a urine PCR of 4200 mg/g has serum albumin 3.8 g/dL and no edema. Per this page, the correct reading is: [The criteria demand nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and/or edema; the 'Also seen in' block names diabetes (m/c) with the bracketed ad]
Hypoalbuminemia in nephrotic syndrome arises from urinary loss of albumin together with: [Urinary loss of albumin; ↓ compensation by liver. (Book p757)]
The nail sign illustrated for hypoalbuminemia, a white transverse line, is: [Sign: white transverse line – Muehrcke's line. (Book p757)]
For nephrotic edema the book ranks the theories as: [Underfill theory > overfill theory. (Book p757)]

The underfill sequence runs hypoalbuminemia → loss of capillary oncotic pressure → fluid transfer to interstitium, giving periorbital puffiness and pedal edema plus: [↓ effective circulatory volume → 2° RAS activation → aldosterone → Na+, water retention. (Book p757)]

Fill up: In the underfill theory, 2° RAS activation causes release of ______, retaining Na+ and water as intravascular edema. [2° RAS activation → release of aldosterone → retention of Na+, water. (Book p757)]

Which of these belongs to the RIGHT-hand branch of the underfill flowchart rather than the left-hand one? [After 'Transfer of fluid from capillaries to interstitium' the chart splits: left to periorbital puffiness and pedal edema (extravascular edema), righ]

Fill up: In the underfill chain, the step that sits between secondary RAS activation and retention of sodium and water is the release of ______. [The printed right-hand chain is ↓ effective circulatory volume → 2° RAS activation → Release of aldosterone → Retention of Na+, water (Intravascular e]

A nephrotic child has periorbital puffiness, pedal edema, pulse 130 and blood pressure 78/50. The underfill chart accounts for the low pressure by: [In underfill, loss of capillary oncotic pressure shifts fluid to the interstitium; the same shift that produces extravascular edema drops the effectiv]

The hypoalbuminemia block gives two mechanisms: urinary loss of albumin and reduced compensation by the liver. [The two bullets read 'urinary loss of albumin' and '↓ compensation by liver'; the nail figure beneath the Sign heading shows Muehrcke's line. (Book p7]

elements.source: The overfill theory is seen in nephritic syndrome; its pathogenesis starts with β hemolytic streptococci releasing plasmin, which activates: [β hemolytic streptococci → plasmin → activates ENaC → 1° RAS activation → retention of Na+, water. (Book p758)]
The second overfill-theory mechanism listed is: [2. ANP resistance. (Book p758)]

The printed pathogenesis of the overfill theory runs in which order? [Overfill theory, seen in nephritic syndrome: 1. β hemolytic streptococci releases plasmin → activates epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) → 1° RAS activa]

The overfill pathway is labelled with PRIMARY RAS activation, in contrast to the SECONDARY activation written in the underfill chart. [p757 underfill ends in ↓ effective circulatory volume → 2° RAS activation; p758 overfill goes ENaC → 1° RAS activation → Na+/water retention (Intravas]

Fill up: In the overfill chain, the streptococcal product that activates the epithelial sodium channel is ______. [The arrows read: β hemolytic streptococci → Releases plasmin → Activates epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). (Book p758)]

Which pair is written in the third management box as 'Rare'? [The management row has three boxes: MCD (85–90%, steroid responsive 95%, no role of biopsy), FSGS (genetic form unresponsive to steroid; Rx renal tran]
The minimal change disease box states 85-90% with steroid responsiveness of 95%; about biopsy it says: [MCD: 85-90%; Rx steroid responsive (95%); no role of biopsy. (Book p758)]
The genetic form of FSGS is unresponsive to steroid; its treatment box lists: [FSGS genetic form: unresponsive to steroid; Rx: renal transplantation. MN, IgA: rare. (Book p758)]
Thrombosis (renal vessel thrombosis, CVT, DVT) becomes a risk when serum albumin falls below: [If serum albumin <2 g/dl → renal vessel thrombosis, CVT, DVT. (Book p758)]

Listed causes of thrombosis include loss of antithrombin III and of protein C/S in urine, ↑ platelet aggregation, ↑ fibrinogen and ↓ plasminogen; the odd one out is: [The book lists ↓ plasminogen, not ↑ plasminogen. (Book p758)]
Albumin is corrected (to >2 g/dL) using 20% albumin (20 g/100 ml) at a dose of: [20% albumin: 20 g/100 ml; dose: 0.5 g/kg. (Book p758)]
Besides 20% albumin, the book notes that these can also be used: [FFP and egg white can also be used. (Book p758)]

Match each haemostatic variable with the direction printed for it in the causes of thrombosis — 1) Antithrombin III and protein C/S 2) Fibrinogen 3) Plasminogen … A) Lost in urine B) Increased C) Decreased D) Unchanged [The block reads: loss of antithrombin III in urine, loss of protein C,S in urine, ↑platelet aggregation, ↑fibrinogen and ↓plasminogen. (Book p758)]

A child with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome has serum albumin 1.4 g/dL and suddenly passes cola-coloured urine with left loin pain. The page's warning that fits best is: [Under Risk of thrombosis the page states: if serum albumin <2 g/dl → can lead to renal vessel thrombosis, CVT, DVT; loin pain with macroscopic haematu]

Match each edema manifestation with its severity label — 1) Ascites 2) Pleural effusion 3) Pericardial effusion … A) Mild B) Rare, with disproportional dyspnoea C) Moderate to severe [Ascites (moderate to severe); pleural effusion (mild); pericardial effusion (rare) with disproportional dyspnoea. (Book p758)]
For moderate-to-severe ascites the book lists ascitic fluid tapping; the m/c cause of death written is: [Rx: ascitic fluid tapping; m/c cause of death: pneumococcal peritonitis. (Book p758)]
A rare pericardial effusion presenting with disproportional dyspnoea is investigated with: [Pericardial effusion (rare): disproportional dyspnoea → Ix: echo. (Book p758)]

elements.source: The dietary prescription for edema is salt restriction below 2 g/day with protein at: [Salt restriction <2 g/day; protein 1 g/kg/day; albumin, FFP. (Book p759)]
Diuretics are avoided in nephrotic edema; they are indicated only when: [Diuretics avoided; indicated only if IVC is non-collapsible in USG; reason: precipitates pre-renal AKI. (Book p759)]
Daily monitoring of the nephrotic child includes weight, urine routine examination and: [Daily monitoring: weight; urine routine examination; urine protein creatinine ratio. (Book p759)]

The steroid regimen written is oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (or 60 mg/m²/day) for 6 weeks with a maximum of 80 mg/day, followed by: [Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (or) 60 mg/m²/day × 6 wks, max 80 mg/day → taper × 6 weeks → stop. (Book p759)]
Remission (90-95%) is defined by urine albumin nil or trace for 3 consecutive days plus urine PCR below: [Remission: urine albumin nil or trace × 3 consecutive days; urine PCR <200 mg/g. (Book p759)]
The proportion labelled steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) at this step is: [Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS): 5-10%. (Book p759)]
Which statement about nephrotic hyperlipidemia is TRUE as written? [Resolves with steroid therapy; no risk of atherosclerosis; no role for statin. (Book p759)]

Match each hyperlipidemia mechanism with its consequence — 1) ↑ lipoprotein lipase 2) ↓ lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) 3) ↑ VLDL, LDL synthesis by liver … A) ↑ VLDL, ↑ LDL, ↑ total cholesterol B) ↑ TG C) ↓ HDL [↑ lipoprotein lipase → ↑ TG; ↓ LCAT → ↓ HDL; ↑ hepatic VLDL/LDL synthesis → ↑ VLDL, ↑ LDL, ↑ total cholesterol. (Book p759)]
The HDL fall in nephrotic hyperlipidemia is attributed to: [D/t loss of HDL in urine: ↓ HDL. (Book p759)]
The associated skin features illustrated with hyperlipidemia are: [Associated features: xanthoma, xanthelasma. (Book p759)]

elements.source: SRNS is proteinuria despite full-dose steroid for 4 weeks; the next step, called the 1st indication in a child, is: [Proteinuria despite full dose of steroid for 4 wk → biopsy (1st indication in child). (Book p760)]
The genetic form of FSGS uncovered on biopsy carries a mutation in: [Genetic form of FSGS (podocin mutation) → Rx: renal transplantation. (Book p760)]

When biopsy shows minimal change disease in SRNS, the DOC are calcineurin inhibitors given for 6 months with a maximum duration of: [Calcineurin inhibitors (DOC): duration 6 months; max 2 yrs. (Book p760)]

Match each calcineurin-inhibitor fact with its label — 1) Tacrolimus dose 2) Tacrolimus side effects 3) Cyclosporine side effects … A) Hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia B) Neuropathy, DM, alopecia C) 0.1 mg/kg/day [Tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day with neuropathy, DM, alopecia; cyclosporine with hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia. (Book p760)]
The first relapse definition in the flowchart is proteinuria appearing after: [Relapse: proteinuria after 1 month of steroid. (Book p760)]
After the first relapse the cohort splits into no-further-relapse, infrequent relapse and FRNS in the proportions: [25% no further relapse; 25% infrequent relapse; 50% FRNS. (Book p760)]
Infrequent relapse is treated with steroid, tapered over 4 weeks: [Infrequent relapse → steroid → taper over 4 wks during remission. (Book p760)]
Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome (FRNS) is defined by: [FRNS: ≥ 2 relapse within 6 months; ≥ 4 relapse within 1 year. (Book p760)]

The steroid-sparing regimen written for FRNS (to prevent steroid toxicity) is oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day × 12 weeks plus steroid × 2 weeks, or: [Steroid sparing drug: oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day × 12 wks + steroid × 2 wks; oral levamisole. (Book p760)]
The second relapse line defines relapse as proteinuria reappearing after: [Relapse: proteinuria reappears after 1 month of intermission. (Book p760)]

Steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome (SDNS) needs ≥ 2 consecutive relapses during tapering of steroid or within how many days after stopping steroid? [SDNS: ≥ 2 consecutive relapses during tapering of steroid (or) within 14 days after stopping steroid. (Book p760)]
The treatment written for SDNS is MMF 1200 mg/m²/day plus: [Treatment: MMF 1200 mg/m²/day; rituximab 375 mg/m²/day × 4 doses. (Book p760)]

elements.source: Adult nephrotic syndrome is summarized as proteinuria with urine PCR ≥3000 mg/d together with: [Proteinuria (urine PCR ≥3000 mg/d); edema; hypoalbuminemia. (Book p761)]
The m/c cause of adult nephrotic syndrome in the cause list is: [Causes: membranous nephropathy (m/c); FSGS; MCD (15%); IgA; MPGN; 2° amyloidosis. (Book p761)]
The adult causes grouped under the 'Rare' bracket are: [Rare bracket: membrano proliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), 2° amyloidosis. (Book p761)]
The adult management sequence is biopsy first, then: [Management: 1. biopsy; 2. rule out 2° causes (Eg: paraneoplastic syndrome). (Book p761)]
The adult steroid trial written is 1 mg/kg/d for: [Steroid: 1 mg/kg/d × 4 months; no response → SRNS. (Book p761)]
An adult failing the 4-month steroid course is labelled SRNS, whose m/c cause is: [No response → SRNS (m/c: FSGS). (Book p761)]
The note's Maltese crosses in polarized light and oval fat bodies are both annotated as seen in: [Maltese crosses in polarized light and oval fat bodies: seen in Fabry's disease. (Book p761)]
In adults, MCD accounts for about what share of nephrotic syndrome? [MCD (15%) among adult causes. (Book p761)]
